description: Production Git troubleshooting runbook focused on the commands that resolve 90% of day-to-day version-control incidents, bad deploys, and on-call recovery scenarios.

commands.title: Show working tree status
commands.summary: Displays the current branch, staged/unstaged changes, and untracked files.
commands.problem: What is the current state of this repository? Am I on the right branch? Are there uncommitted changes that will block a deploy or merge?
commands.why_this_command: The single most important first command in any Git incident. Everything else depends on knowing the exact state of the working tree and HEAD.
thinking_process: Something looks wrong with the code on this host or in this PR.
git status tells me the branch, whether it is clean, and what is staged or modified.
From there I decide whether to commit, stash, reset, or switch branches.
commands.expected_output:
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
nothing to commit, working tree clean
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Look at the branch name first. Then check for 'Changes to be committed', 'Changes not staged', and 'Untracked files'. A dirty tree on a production checkout is almost always a problem.
real_world_incidents: Deploy failed because uncommitted local changes existed on the build agent.
Engineer was on a feature branch instead of main when investigating a production bug.
Leftover untracked config files caused a service to pick up the wrong settings.
common_mistakes: Assuming the working tree is clean without running status.
Ignoring untracked files that are actually required by the application.
Not noticing that the branch has diverged from its remote.
what_to_check_before: Confirm you are in the correct repository directory.
what_to_check_after: If on the wrong branch → git checkout or git switch
If dirty → decide to commit, stash, or discard
If behind/ahead → git fetch and then pull or push
best_practices: Always run git status as the first command when you enter a repository during an incident.
Use git status -sb for a compact view in scripts and busy terminals.
commands.interview_question: You open a repository and need to know immediately whether it is safe to pull. What do you run first and why?
commands.interview_answer: git status. It shows the current branch, whether the working tree is clean, and how the branch relates to its upstream. A dirty tree or divergence must be resolved before pulling.

commands.title: Show commit history
commands.summary: Displays the commit history with messages, authors, and hashes.
commands.problem: What changed recently? Who introduced this commit? What is the exact commit currently deployed?
commands.why_this_command: Essential for tracing regressions, verifying deploys, and finding the commit to revert or bisect.
thinking_process: Production broke after a deploy.
git log shows the recent commits and their messages.
I can identify the suspect commit and then inspect or revert it.
commands.expected_output: commit hashes, authors, dates, and messages (or compact one-line form)
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Look for the most recent commits first. Match deploy times to commit timestamps. Use the hash for subsequent checkout, revert, or bisect.
real_world_incidents: Identifying the exact commit that introduced a breaking API change.
Confirming that a hotfix had actually landed on the production branch.
Finding the author of a change that broke CI.
common_mistakes: Looking only at the message and missing the full diff with -p.
Assuming the top commit is what is running in production without verifying the deployed SHA.
Not limiting output with -n and getting overwhelmed.
what_to_check_before: Know roughly when the problem started.
what_to_check_after: If a bad commit is identified → git show <hash> or git revert
If history is unclear → git log --graph --oneline --all
best_practices: Prefer git log --oneline -20 for rapid incident triage.
Always record the production commit SHA in deploy logs so you can match it later.
commands.interview_question: How do you quickly see the last 5 commits with their hashes and one-line messages?

commands.title: Show changes in the working tree or between commits
commands.summary: Shows unstaged changes, staged changes, or differences between commits.
commands.problem: What exactly changed? Is this the change I expected before committing or deploying?
commands.why_this_command: The only reliable way to review the precise content of modifications before they are committed or after they have been made.
thinking_process: git status showed modified files.
git diff shows the actual line-by-line changes.
I can decide whether to stage, discard, or keep them.
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Red/removed lines are what was deleted; green/added lines are new. Watch for accidental deletions, debug prints, or secrets.
real_world_incidents: Catching a debug print that would have been committed.
Discovering that a config file change was larger than expected.
Comparing the running production commit against the previous one during a regression.
common_mistakes: Looking only at unstaged diff and missing what is already staged.
Forgetting that git diff shows unstaged changes by default.
Not reviewing the full diff of a large change before force-pushing.
what_to_check_before: Run git status first to know what is staged vs unstaged.
what_to_check_after: If changes look good → git add and commit
If changes are wrong → git checkout -- <file> or git restore
best_practices: Always run git diff and git diff --staged before every commit.
Use git diff HEAD~1 during incident review to see exactly what the last commit changed.
commands.interview_question: How do you see only the changes that have already been staged for commit?

commands.title: Switch branches or restore files
commands.summary: Switches branches or restores working-tree files from a commit or the index.
commands.problem: I am on the wrong branch, or I need to discard local changes to a file, or I need to examine an old commit.
commands.why_this_command: Still the most widely used command for branch switching and file restoration in production environments, even though git switch and git restore exist.
thinking_process: git status showed I am on a feature branch or have unwanted local changes.
git checkout <branch> moves me to the correct branch.
git checkout -- <file> discards local modifications safely.
commands.syntax: git checkout <branch> | git checkout -- <file> | git checkout <commit>
commands.expected_output: Switched to branch 'main' or Updated N paths from ...
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Success messages confirm the switch or restore. Detached HEAD warning appears when checking out a commit directly.
real_world_incidents: Moving a production checkout from a feature branch back to main.
Discarding a broken local config change that was causing the service to fail.
Checking out the exact commit that was deployed to reproduce a bug.
common_mistakes: Using git checkout <file> without -- and accidentally creating a branch.
Checking out a commit and ending up in detached HEAD without realizing it.
Discarding changes that were actually needed.
what_to_check_before: git status to see what will be overwritten.
Stash or commit anything you might need later.
what_to_check_after: git status to confirm the new state.
If detached HEAD → create a branch or return to a named branch.
best_practices: Prefer git switch for branch changes and git restore for file restoration when the Git version supports them.
Never discard changes without confirming they are disposable.
commands.interview_question: What is the difference between git checkout main and git checkout abc1234?
commands.interview_answer: git checkout main switches to the named branch and stays on it. git checkout abc1234 puts you in detached HEAD state at that commit; any new commits will be orphaned unless you create a branch.

commands.title: Create or list branches
commands.summary: Lists local branches or creates/deletes a branch.
commands.problem: What branches exist locally? Am I on the expected branch? Do I need a new branch for a hotfix?
commands.why_this_command: Quick way to see branch state and to create a short-lived hotfix branch during an incident.
thinking_process: I need to know which branches are present and which one is current.
git branch shows the list with * marking the current branch.
git branch hotfix/xxx creates a new branch for an emergency fix.
commands.how_to_interpret_output: The asterisk marks the current branch. -a shows remote-tracking branches as well. -v adds the last commit on each branch.
real_world_incidents: Confirming a hotfix branch was created from the correct production commit.
Discovering that a long-lived feature branch was still checked out on a server.
Cleaning up stale local branches after a release.
common_mistakes: Creating a branch without switching to it (git branch only creates; use checkout/switch to move).
Deleting a branch that still has unmerged work with -d vs -D.
Not fetching first, so remote branches are missing from the view.
what_to_check_before: git status to know the current branch and working-tree state.
what_to_check_after: If you created a branch → git checkout <name> or git switch <name>
If cleaning up → git fetch --prune and then delete safely
best_practices: Always create hotfix branches from the exact production commit SHA.
Use descriptive names: hotfix/short-description.
commands.interview_question: How do you create a new branch and switch to it in one command?

commands.title: Fetch remote updates without merging
commands.summary: Downloads commits, branches, and tags from the remote without changing the working tree.
commands.problem: Is the remote ahead of me? What new commits exist on origin before I pull or deploy?
commands.why_this_command: Safe way to update remote-tracking branches so you can inspect what will change before merging or rebasing.
thinking_process: I need to know whether production or origin/main has moved.
git fetch updates the remote-tracking refs.
Then I can log or diff against origin/main safely.
commands.expected_output:
From github.com:org/repo
 * [new branch] ...
   abc..def  main -> origin/main
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Shows which refs were updated. No local branches or working tree are modified. After fetch you can safely compare with origin/main.
real_world_incidents: Discovering that origin/main had moved forward before a planned deploy.
Fetching a hotfix branch that was pushed by another engineer.
Pruning deleted remote branches that were still cluttering the local view.
common_mistakes: Assuming fetch updates the current branch (it does not).
Forgetting --prune and accumulating stale remote-tracking branches.
Fetching and then immediately pulling without reviewing the incoming commits.
what_to_check_after: git log HEAD..origin/main to see what would be merged
git status to see ahead/behind counts
best_practices: Fetch before every pull or rebase so you can review the incoming changes.
Use git fetch --prune regularly to keep remote-tracking branches clean.
commands.interview_question: What is the practical difference between git fetch and git pull?
commands.interview_answer: git fetch only updates remote-tracking branches; the working tree and current branch stay unchanged. git pull does a fetch followed by a merge (or rebase) into the current branch.

commands.title: Integrate remote changes into the current branch
commands.summary: Fetches from the remote and merges (or rebases) into the current branch.
commands.problem: My local branch is behind the remote and I need the latest commits before building or deploying.
commands.why_this_command: The everyday way to bring a tracking branch up to date. Used constantly on developer machines and sometimes on deploy hosts.
thinking_process: git status showed the branch is behind origin.
I have confirmed the working tree is clean.
git pull brings the latest changes in.
commands.expected_output:
Updating abc..def
Fast-forward
 or a merge commit message
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Fast-forward is cleanest. A merge commit means histories diverged. Conflicts will stop the pull and require resolution.
real_world_incidents: Pulling the latest main onto a deploy host before a release.
Merge conflicts appearing because local commits existed that were not expected.
Accidentally pulling into a dirty working tree and creating a mess.
common_mistakes: Pulling with a dirty working tree.
Using pull on a production server that should only ever check out a specific SHA.
Not reviewing the incoming commits before the pull completes.
what_to_check_before: Prefer git fetch + review before a plain pull on shared or production branches.
what_to_check_after: git status and git log -5 to confirm the new state.
If conflicts → resolve, git add, git commit (or git rebase --continue)
best_practices: On shared branches prefer git pull --rebase to avoid unnecessary merge commits.
Never pull on a production checkout that is expected to be at a pinned SHA; check out the SHA instead.
commands.interview_question: When is git pull --rebase preferable to a plain git pull?
commands.interview_answer: When you have local commits that have not been pushed and you want a linear history instead of a merge commit. It replays your commits on top of the updated remote branch.

commands.title: Temporarily shelve local changes
commands.summary: Saves uncommitted changes and reverts the working tree to a clean state.
commands.problem: I have local modifications but need a clean tree to switch branches, pull, or deploy, and I do not want to commit yet.
commands.why_this_command: The standard way to set aside work-in-progress without creating a commit that will later need to be cleaned up.
thinking_process: git status shows modified files I am not ready to commit.
I need to switch branches or pull.
git stash saves the changes and cleans the tree; I can pop them later.
commands.syntax: git stash [push] [-m message] | git stash list | git stash pop
commands.expected_output: Saved working directory and index state ...
commands.how_to_interpret_output: The working tree becomes clean. git stash list shows the stack of stashes. pop reapplies the most recent and removes it from the stack.
real_world_incidents: Stashing debug changes so a clean pull could be performed on a shared server.
Recovering work that would otherwise have been lost when switching branches under time pressure.
Accidentally dropping a stash that contained important local fixes.
common_mistakes: Stashing and then forgetting the stash exists.
Using git stash drop on the wrong entry.
Stashing untracked files without -u and losing them.
what_to_check_before: git status to know exactly what will be stashed.
what_to_check_after: git status should now be clean.
When ready → git stash pop or git stash apply
git stash list to confirm what remains
best_practices: Always add a message with -m so you can identify the stash later.
Prefer git stash apply over pop if you want to keep the stash as a backup until you are sure.
commands.interview_question: How do you stash both tracked and untracked files?

commands.title: Undo the last commit while keeping changes
commands.summary: Moves HEAD (and optionally the index and working tree) to a different commit.
commands.problem: I committed too early, committed on the wrong branch, or need to unstage changes. I want to undo the commit but keep the work.
commands.why_this_command: The primary tool for safely rewriting local history before it has been pushed. Essential for recovering from 'oops' commits.
thinking_process: I just made a commit that should not have been made yet, or it contains the wrong files.
git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the commit but leaves everything staged.
git reset HEAD~1 (mixed) undoes the commit and unstages but keeps the files modified.
commands.expected_output: Usually silent; working tree and index change according to the mode.
commands.how_to_interpret_output: After --soft the changes remain staged. After mixed (default) they become unstaged. After --hard they are discarded entirely.
real_world_incidents: Undoing a commit that accidentally included a secret before it was pushed.
Moving a commit from a feature branch back to unstaged changes so it could be recommitted correctly.
Hard-resetting a deploy host to the exact origin/main state after manual experimentation.
common_mistakes: Using --hard and permanently losing uncommitted work.
Resetting commits that have already been pushed and then force-pushing without coordination.
Confusing soft/mixed/hard modes.
what_to_check_before: Confirm the commits have not been pushed, or that a force-push is acceptable.
git status and git log -3 to know exactly what will be affected.
what_to_check_after: git status and git log to verify the new state.
If you need the changes again → they should still be in the working tree (unless --hard).
best_practices: Prefer --soft or mixed for local recovery. Use --hard only when you are certain the changes are disposable.
Never reset public history without team agreement; use git revert instead.
commands.interview_question: What is the difference between git reset --soft HEAD~1 and git reset --hard HEAD~1?
commands.interview_answer: --soft moves HEAD back one commit but leaves the index and working tree exactly as they were (changes stay staged). --hard moves HEAD and also resets the index and working tree, discarding the changes completely.

commands.title: Create a new commit that undoes a previous one
commands.summary: Generates a new commit that reverses the changes introduced by a specified commit.
commands.problem: A bad commit has already been pushed and shared. I need to undo its effects without rewriting history.
commands.why_this_command: The safe, history-preserving way to undo changes on shared branches. Preferred over reset for any commit that has left your machine.
thinking_process: A commit on main is causing a production incident and has already been pulled by others.
git revert <hash> creates a new commit that applies the opposite diff.
I can then push the revert commit normally.
commands.expected_output: Opens an editor for the revert commit message, then creates the new commit.
commands.how_to_interpret_output: A new commit appears on top of history whose diff is the inverse of the original. Conflicts may occur if later commits touched the same lines.
real_world_incidents: Reverting a bad configuration change that had already been deployed and pulled by the whole team.
Reverting a merge commit that introduced a regression.
Quickly undoing a hotfix that itself introduced a new bug.
common_mistakes: Trying to revert a merge commit without -m.
Reverting and then also resetting, creating confusion.
Not testing the reverted state before pushing.
what_to_check_before: Confirm the exact commit hash with git log.
Ensure the working tree is clean.
what_to_check_after: git log -2 and git show HEAD to verify the revert commit.
Run tests or deploy the reverted state.
Push the new commit.
best_practices: Always prefer revert over reset for commits that have been pushed.
Use a clear commit message that references the original commit and the reason for the revert.
commands.interview_question: Why is git revert safer than git reset for undoing a commit that is already on origin/main?
commands.interview_answer: git revert adds a new commit that undoes the changes, preserving history and not requiring a force-push. git reset rewrites history and forces everyone else to recover, which is dangerous on shared branches.

commands.title: Inspect a specific commit or object
commands.summary: Shows the metadata and diff of a commit, or the contents of any Git object.
commands.problem: What exactly did this commit change? What is the full message and author information?
commands.why_this_command: The fastest way to examine a single commit in detail during a regression or code review under pressure.
thinking_process: git log identified a suspicious commit hash.
git show <hash> displays the full message and the complete diff.
I can decide whether to revert, cherry-pick, or dig further.
commands.expected_output: Commit header (author, date, message) followed by the full unified diff
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Read the message first, then the diff. --stat gives a high-level file-change summary when the full diff is too large.
real_world_incidents: Confirming that a commit only touched the expected files before deciding to revert.
Finding a secret that had been committed by examining the diff.
Understanding the exact change that caused a test failure.
common_mistakes: Running git show without a hash and assuming it shows something other than HEAD.
Not using --stat first on large commits and getting flooded with output.
what_to_check_before: Have the commit hash from git log or a CI failure.
what_to_check_after: If the change is bad → git revert
If more context is needed → git log -p or git blame on the affected files
best_practices: Use git show --stat <hash> first for large commits.
Combine with git log --oneline to move quickly between candidates.
commands.interview_question: How do you see both the commit message and the full diff of the previous commit?

commands.title: Recover lost commits or find previous HEAD positions
commands.summary: Shows a log of where HEAD and branch tips have pointed, including commits that are no longer reachable.
commands.problem: I accidentally reset, rebased, or deleted a branch and need to recover commits that seem gone.
commands.why_this_command: The safety net for almost every destructive Git operation. If a commit was ever checked out or committed locally, reflog can usually find it.
thinking_process: I ran a hard reset or deleted a branch and now the commits appear lost.
git reflog lists every recent movement of HEAD.
I can check out or reset back to the reflog entry that still has my work.
commands.expected_output:
HEAD@{0}: commit: message
HEAD@{1}: reset: moving to ...
 etc.
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Each line is a previous position of HEAD. The higher the number, the older the entry. Find the entry just before the destructive action and recover from there.
real_world_incidents: Recovering commits after an accidental git reset --hard.
Restoring a branch that was deleted locally before it was pushed.
Finding the previous HEAD after a bad rebase.
common_mistakes: Waiting too long; reflog entries expire (default 90 days for reachable, 30 for unreachable).
Confusing reflog with the regular commit log.
Checking out a reflog entry and then losing it again by not creating a branch.
what_to_check_before: Act quickly after realizing the mistake.
what_to_check_after: Once the good commit is identified → git branch recover/<name> <hash> or git reset --hard <hash>
Verify with git log that the work is back.
best_practices: Treat reflog as your undo history for Git itself.
As soon as you recover a commit, create a named branch so it does not become unreachable again.
commands.interview_question: You just ran git reset --hard HEAD~3 and realized you needed those commits. How do you get them back?
commands.interview_answer: Run git reflog, find the entry that pointed to the commit before the reset (usually HEAD@{1}), then git reset --hard HEAD@{1} or create a branch from that hash.
